slides.title: What does attention compute?
slides.body:
Look at the heatmap on the right. Each row is a **query** (the token "asking the question"), and each column is a **key** (the token "advertising itself"). Brighter cells mean stronger attention.

Notice the row for **`are`** — almost all the weight sits on **`cats`**. The verb knows it has to agree with its subject several tokens back. That's not a hand-coded rule; it emerges from training on lots of grammatical text.

The whole point of attention: every token gets to **look at every other token**, weighted by relevance, and combine their information in a single mathematical operation.

slides.title: Three vectors per token
slides.body:
Mechanically, attention works by giving each token three projections of itself:

- **Query (Q):** "What am I looking for?"
- **Key (K):** "What do I have to offer?"
- **Value (V):** "What information do I actually carry?"

The attention score from token *i* to token *j* is the dot product `Q_i · K_j` — high when the query and the key align in the same direction. The softmax of these scores becomes a weight; the weighted sum of values is the output:

$$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{Q K^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$$

The `√d_k` scaling keeps the dot products from blowing up in high dimensions and pushing softmax into a one-hot regime.

slides.title: Locality bias
slides.body:
Different attention heads learn different patterns. This one shows a **locality bias** — each token mostly attends to its immediate neighbors. That's a useful pattern for tasks where nearby context dominates (like syntax) and you'd see some heads in any trained transformer adopt this behavior.

Other heads learn long-range dependencies. Many learn structures we still don't fully understand. Mechanistic interpretability — reverse-engineering what heads do — is a whole research area built on this fact.

question.question: What does the matrix product `Q · Kᵀ` produce?
options: An n×n matrix where entry (i, j) is the similarity score between query i and key j
A scalar — the total attention magnitude
An n-dimensional vector of probabilities over keys
A new embedding for each token, in a different space
question.explanation: Q is [n, d_k], K is [n, d_k], so Q · Kᵀ is [n, n]. Row i column j is the dot product of query i with key j — a similarity score. After scaling by 1/√d_k and applying softmax, this becomes the attention weight matrix.

slides.title: Pronoun resolution
slides.body:
Here's a more linguistically interesting pattern: the pronoun **`she`** attends back to its antecedent **`Maria`**. The model has learned that pronouns need to know what they refer to, and attention is the mechanism that lets it look back.

This isn't a single head's job in a real model — it's a circuit involving multiple heads across multiple layers (Olsson et al. 2022 traced an analogous mechanism for in-context learning). But the pattern is real: trained attention learns linguistic structure.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
We've covered the basic attention computation. Three follow-ups make this practical:

- **[Self-attention](/wiki/self-attention)** — when Q, K, V all come from the same sequence, every token can attend to every other.
- **[Multi-head attention](/wiki/multi-head-attention)** — running several attention computations in parallel, each in a different subspace, lets one layer learn many patterns at once.
- **[Causal masking](/wiki/masked-self-attention)** — for autoregressive generation, the upper triangle of the attention matrix is masked out so future tokens can't leak into past ones.

The rest of the transformer is mostly bookkeeping — but everything important happens in attention.
